content:
It's very easy to forget Id.run and pure when working with the Id monad, resulting in defeq issues when silently casting between X and Id X. While core is now mostly free of these as of lean4#7352, it's still easy for them to end up reappearing in downstream projects, which lead users down dead ends like simp [Id.run, Pure.pure, Bind.bind], leaving them with a bad goal state.

Should Id be redefined as

structure Id (X : Type _) where
  /-- Not simp-normal, use Pure.pure instead. -/
  protected pure ::
  run : X

instance : Pure Id where pure := Id.pure

@[simp] theorem Id.pure_eq : Id.pure = Pure.pure := rfl

such that it is impossible to make this mistake?
What's the difference between using a single element structure and removing @[expose] as a way to prevent defeqs?
With a 1-field structure, you still have .mk a.run = a as a defeq.
Another difference is that for the 1-field structure, Id X = X (or equivalently, Id = id) becomes independent of Lean, which occasionally matters

Yury G. Kudryashov said:

With a 1-field structure, you still have .mk a.run = a as a defeq.

run (pure x) = x is the one we care about
YES please! When I was implementing automatic differentiation for monadic code the defeq abuse was a major pain point. At some point I just gave up an defined my own id monad.
I'd like to see this too, knowing that it continues to trip people up. I am worried that it is quite a breaking change -- does anyone have ideas how we could help people whose code breaks?

Perhaps we could introduce a linter for Id defeq abuse first and let it run for a deprecation period.

Here is a proof of concept: lean4#12758

I bet that this linter has its weaknesses in its current form, and it most certainly overlooks a few abuses that are intermingled with coercions. A more robust approach would be to check for each subexpression of every declaration whether the expected and inferred types are still defeq if Id is made irreducible, but this is probably a bit more expensive than piggy-backing on the existing infotree data. Didn't benchmark it.

(It already found quite a few (> 2000) issues in 175 files of lean4 itself. Some of them are fine, like those in Init.Control.Id, but most probably aren't. I checked the first few of them so far and these warnings seem to be pointing out real abuse.)
Would tagging Id as @[irreducible] be strictly less of a breaking change than making it a structure? That could be used to check if code breaks.
Alternatively, is there any way to keep the run (pure x) = x defeq with the module system?
It's more of a breaking change. With a structure, you still have run (pure x) = x.

I see, that makes sense. One thing I am worried about with this change is that it makes Id behave in a way I wouldn't expect it to, which is that it actually changes the type to something not equal to it (definitionally or propositionally), and it will behave significantly differently from id (I would expect id and Id to behave the same). If the sole purpose of Id is to be used as a monad and other uses aren't supported, this should be communicated to the user, e.g. by changing its name to IdM.
Introducing IdM would make the deprecation straightforward

On the other hand, migrating libraries seems more difficult when having Id and IdM at the same time. At some point, the standard library (e.g., iterators) would need to switch from using Id to using IdM in its public-facing API, and having this parallel structure can be very confusing.

One thing I am a bit worried about is that many basic monads like StateM, ReaderM etc. are defined as monad transformers applied to the Id monad. Making Id more complex could make working with these basic monads more clumsy.
I think a lot of those transformers should also be one-field structures...
(I have an open draft PR to lean4 that makes the use of mk and run more consistent)

I don't mind what they are under the hood but StateM.run' should return the value, and not the value wrapped into something. Currently StateM.run' is not defined but (program : StateM S).run' start expands to calling StateT.run' : StateM S -> S -> Id Value
I do like the fact that ReaderT is a def. I can write x c rather than ReaderT.run x c when dot notation doesn't work (e.g. if x : MetaM _)
Why would dot notation not work there?
If ctx : Meta.Context, ref : IO.Ref Meta.State and x : MetaM α, it can be handy to write x ctx ref

Eric Wieser said:

I think a lot of those transformers should also be one-field structures...

While I'd love for them to be structures, as far as I know, most monad types like StateM need to be equal to function types at this point. Consider a recursive monadic function such as:

def f (n : Nat) : StateM Nat Nat :=
  match n with
  | 0 => get
  | n' + 1 => f n' -- (f n') : Nat → Nat × Nat

Without optimizations, recursive monadic functions would return a lambda function representing the monadic element. This only does not happen because the compiler sees that the return type of the recursive function is a function type, and therefore eta-expands it.

For example, this generates bad code:

structure StateM' (α β : Type) where
  inner : StateM α β

instance : Monad (StateM' σ) where
  pure a := ⟨pure a⟩
  bind x f := ⟨x.inner >>= (fun a => (f a).inner)⟩

set_option trace.Compiler.result true in
def f' (n : Nat) : StateM' Nat Nat :=
  match n with
  | 0 => return 0
  | n' + 1 => f' n' -- (f n') : Nat → Nat × Nat

Niels Voss said:

Would tagging Id as @[irreducible] be strictly less of a breaking change than making it a structure? That could be used to check if code breaks.

Yury G. Kudryashov said:

It's more of a breaking change. With a structure, you still have run (pure x) = x.

Id being irreducible doesn't make Id.run and pure irreducible, so the definitional equalities still work (although I'm afraid of finding out how reliably this works):

set_option allowUnsafeReducibility true in
attribute [irreducible] Id

theorem Id.run_pure' {x : α} :
    Id.run (pure x) = x :=
  rfl
